cueCard.title: Describe a person you know who is good at cooking.
points: what kinds of food he or she cooks
how he or she learned to cook
cueCard.final: and explain why you think this person is a good cook.

sample:
I'd like to talk about my dad, who is easily the best cook in our family, although he'd never say so himself. He's quite a quiet man and not very good at expressing his feelings, but in the kitchen he becomes a completely different person.

Most of what he cooks is home-style southern food. He makes a steamed fish with ginger and spring onion that I still haven't found anywhere else, and his braised pork is so tender you could cut it with a spoon. He's also brilliant at soups, which he simmers for hours on Sunday afternoons. Whenever I go home, there's always a pot of something waiting on the stove, even if I arrive close to midnight.

Interestingly, he never learned from a cookbook or a class. When he was a teenager, both his parents worked long shifts at a factory, so he had to cook for his younger sister every day. At first it was mostly plain noodles, but he gradually picked up tricks by watching neighbours and asking stallholders at the market how they made certain dishes. Even now, if he eats something good at a restaurant, he'll try to recreate it at home the following weekend.

What makes him a good cook, in my opinion, is that he really pays attention. He knows exactly how much salt my mum likes, and he remembers which dishes I loved as a child. For him, cooking is a way of showing care without having to say anything. I've tried to copy some of his recipes in my tiny kitchen, but somehow they never taste quite the same.

part3.q: Why do fewer young people cook at home nowadays?
part3.sample: There are several reasons. The most obvious is time. Many young people work long hours and have long commutes, so by the time they get home, cooking feels like a chore. Delivery apps have also made takeaways cheap and incredibly convenient. Another factor is that many of them grew up with parents or grandparents doing all the cooking, so they never really learned. Small rented flats with tiny kitchens don't help either.

part3.q: Is home cooking an important part of family life?
part3.sample: I think it is, or at least sharing meals is. When a family cooks and eats together, it creates a regular time to talk, which is increasingly rare when everyone is busy with their own screens. Children also learn about food, health and even family history through recipes passed down from older relatives. Of course, it doesn't have to be elaborate. Even a simple dinner at home a few times a week can make a real difference to how connected a family feels.

part3.q: Do you think traditional recipes will be lost in the future?
part3.sample: Some of them probably will. Many traditional dishes take hours to prepare and rely on knowledge that was passed on by watching older relatives rather than written down. If young people stop cooking, that chain breaks. On the other hand, the internet is full of cooking videos, and some young people are now deliberately recording their grandparents' recipes. So I'd expect the most popular dishes to survive, while very local or time-consuming ones may gradually disappear.

part3.q: Why have cooking programmes and food videos become so popular?
part3.sample: Partly because food is something everyone can relate to. You don't need any special knowledge to enjoy watching someone make dumplings. These videos are also very relaxing, since the process is satisfying and usually ends successfully, unlike a lot of real life. Interestingly, many viewers never actually cook the dishes. For them, it's more like entertainment or a form of armchair travel, because they can see how people eat in other regions and countries.

cueCard.title: Describe a person you know who speaks a foreign language very well.
points: which language he or she speaks
how he or she learned it
cueCard.final: and explain how you feel about this person's language ability.

sample:
The person I'd like to describe is Qiao, a colleague who works in our company's international sales team. She's in her mid-thirties, and she's the one everyone turns to when we have clients from Latin America, because she speaks fluent Spanish.

What struck me when I first heard her was how natural she sounds. I don't speak a word of Spanish myself, but during video calls with clients in Mexico and Chile, she laughs at their jokes, makes jokes of her own and switches between Spanish, English and Chinese without any obvious effort. Clients often assume she's lived in Latin America for years.

In fact, she's never lived abroad at all. She studied engineering at university and only started Spanish in her late twenties, after getting hooked on a Spanish-language TV series. At first she just used a free app on her commute, but then she found a language exchange partner online, a teacher from Colombia who wanted to learn Chinese. They've been talking twice a week for about six years now. She also reads Spanish news every morning and has even switched her phone to Spanish, which she says forces her to think in it.

I find her ability really inspiring, but also a bit humbling. Like a lot of Chinese students, I learned English mostly from textbooks, and I still sometimes freeze when a conversation goes in an unexpected direction. Qiao proves that you don't need to be young or live abroad to become fluent. What you need is regular, genuine conversation, and lately I've been trying to follow her example.

part3.q: Why do some people find it easier to learn foreign languages than others?
part3.sample: Several factors are involved. Some people seem to have a natural ear for sounds, so they pick up pronunciation more easily. Personality matters too. Outgoing people who don't mind making mistakes tend to get far more speaking practice than shy perfectionists. But I think motivation is the biggest factor. Someone who's learning a language because they love the culture, or need it for a job they really want, will keep going long after others have given up.

part3.q: Is it better to start learning a foreign language as a child?
part3.sample: In general, yes, especially for pronunciation. Young children can imitate sounds very accurately, and they're less afraid of sounding silly. However, adults have advantages too. They can understand grammar rules, use learning strategies and set clear goals, and plenty of adults reach a very high level. So starting early helps, but it's not the only route. Besides, an unhappy child forced into lessons may end up hating the language altogether.

part3.q: Will translation technology make learning foreign languages unnecessary?
part3.sample: I don't think so, although it will change why people learn. Translation apps are already good enough for ordering food or reading a sign, and they're likely to keep improving. But a language is more than a tool for exchanging information. Humour, tone and cultural references are often lost in machine translation, and building real relationships is hard when every conversation goes through a device. So people may learn languages less out of necessity and more for connection.

part3.q: Should everyone be required to learn a second language at school?
part3.sample: In principle, I think it's a good idea. Learning another language opens doors to jobs and travel, and it also helps students realise that their own way of seeing the world isn't the only one. In China, English is already compulsory from primary school. The problem is how it's taught. If lessons focus only on grammar for exams, students can study for ten years and still be unable to hold a conversation, which seems like a huge waste of effort.

cueCard.title: Describe a neighbour you remember from your childhood.
cueCard.final: and explain why you remember this neighbour so well.

sample:
I'd like to talk about Auntie Chen, who lived across the landing from us in the old building where I grew up. In China, children often call older neighbours auntie or uncle, even though they're not related, and for me she really did feel like part of the family.

The building belonged to my dad's work unit, so everyone knew each other, and front doors were left open most of the time. Auntie Chen was a nurse at the local hospital, and she lived with her husband and their son, who was a few years older than me. Their flat was exactly the same size as ours, but it always seemed livelier, with a radio playing and the smell of something cooking.

Because my parents often worked late, I'd go over to her place after school. She made me sit at her kitchen table and finish my homework before I was allowed to watch cartoons, and she was far stricter about it than my own mum. In return, she fed me, and her red bean soup in summer was legendary. Sometimes she took me with her to the vegetable market and let me choose what we'd have for dinner, which made me feel very grown-up.

I think I remember her so clearly because she was the first adult outside my family who looked after me. She taught me small but important things, like how to clean a cut properly and why you should always thank the person who cooks. When we moved to a new area, I cried for days. We still visit her at Spring Festival, and she still asks whether I've done my homework.

part3.q: Why do people in cities often not know their neighbours?
part3.sample: One reason is that people move much more often now, especially renters, so there seems little point in building relationships. Modern high-rise buildings also aren't designed for socialising. You take the lift straight from the car park to your door and rarely pass anyone. And long working hours mean people come home tired and want privacy. In the past, shared kitchens or courtyards forced neighbours to interact, but most new housing has no spaces like that.

part3.q: What can be done to build a stronger sense of community in neighbourhoods?
part3.sample: Shared spaces are a good start. A small garden, a playground or a community room gives people a natural reason to meet. Local events help as well, like a weekend market or a celebration during festivals. Some residents' committees in China organise activities for children and older people, and online group chats can break the ice, as long as they lead to face-to-face contact. Ultimately, though, it takes residents who are willing to make the first move.

part3.q: Is it important for children to grow up with a strong community around them?
part3.sample: I believe it matters a great deal. When children know lots of adults nearby, they feel safer and have more people to turn to if something goes wrong. They also learn social skills by dealing with people of different ages, not just their parents and classmates. A close community can share the job of keeping an eye on kids, which helps working parents. Without it, children may spend more time alone at home with screens, which isn't ideal for anyone.

part3.q: How might relationships between neighbours change in the future?
part3.sample: I expect them to become more digital. Many housing estates already have group chats where people share information, sell second-hand items or warn each other about problems. That trend will probably continue, and apps might even match neighbours who want to share tools or childcare. At the same time, as the population ages, neighbours could become more important again, because elderly people living alone will rely on those nearby for everyday help and company.

cueCard.title: Describe a shop you enjoy visiting.
cueCard.final: and explain why you enjoy visiting this shop.

sample:
The shop I'd like to talk about is a tiny second-hand camera shop in the old town, tucked between a noodle restaurant and a key-cutting stall. From the outside it doesn't look like much, just a narrow glass door and a faded sign, so most people walk straight past it.

Inside, it's crammed from floor to ceiling with old cameras, lenses and all kinds of accessories, some of them more than fifty years old. There are heavy film cameras that look as if they could survive being run over by a bus, as well as more recent digital models. The owner, Mr He, is a retired newspaper photographer in his late sixties. He repairs everything himself at a small workbench at the back, surrounded by tiny screwdrivers and jars of screws.

I first went there about two years ago, when I'd decided to move on from my phone camera but couldn't afford anything new. Mr He spent nearly an hour asking what I liked to photograph before recommending a second-hand camera that suited my budget, and I've been using it ever since. These days I drop in about once a month, sometimes to buy a filter or have my lens cleaned, but often just to chat.

What I enjoy most is the atmosphere. Nobody tries to sell you anything you don't need, and Mr He is always happy to share tips about composition or tell stories about the photographers who used to work in the city. Browsing online reduces everything to prices and star ratings, whereas visiting his shop feels like a conversation. I'd be genuinely sad if it ever closed.

part3.q: Why do some people prefer small independent shops to large chain stores?
part3.sample: Mainly for the personal touch. In a small shop, the owner often knows the products inside out and remembers regular customers, which makes shopping feel more human. Independent shops also tend to stock unusual items you won't find anywhere else. Some people support them for ethical reasons as well, because the money stays in the local community rather than going to a large corporation. Chain stores are cheaper and more convenient, but they can feel rather impersonal.

part3.q: How has online shopping affected traditional shops?
part3.sample: It's hit many of them hard. Shops selling standard products, like electronics or books, struggle to compete with online prices and next-day delivery, and quite a few have closed in my city. However, the ones that survive have often adapted cleverly. Some now sell online as well, while others focus on things the internet can't offer, such as expert advice, workshops or a pleasant place to spend time. So online shopping has forced high streets to change rather than simply killing them.

part3.q: Should local governments help small shops to survive?
part3.sample: I think there's a case for some support. Small shops give neighbourhoods character, and they provide jobs and services, especially for elderly residents who don't shop online. Rents in city centres have risen so much that even popular family businesses can be forced out. Governments could offer lower rents in public buildings or tax breaks for traditional trades. However, they shouldn't keep failing businesses alive artificially. If a shop isn't meeting people's needs, something new may deserve the space.

part3.q: What do you think shopping will be like in the future?
part3.sample: I expect it to become even more personalised. Shops will probably use data and artificial intelligence to recommend products before we even know we want them, and in some areas deliveries might be made by drones or robots. Physical shops are likely to become more like showrooms or social spaces, where people go to try things and meet friends rather than just to buy. There might also be more interest in second-hand goods and repairs, as people worry more about waste.

cueCard.title: Describe a market you like to visit.
points: who you usually go there with
cueCard.final: and explain why you like this market.

sample:
I'd like to describe the night market near my old secondary school in my hometown. It's held every evening on a long street that's used by ordinary traffic during the day, and from about six o'clock, dozens of stalls appear as if by magic.

Most of the stalls sell food, which is the main reason people go. There are rice noodles in spicy broth, grilled squid on sticks, oyster omelettes and sweet soups with taro and coconut milk. Further along, there are stalls selling cheap phone cases, clothes, toys and household bits and pieces, along with a man who has been fixing watches on the same corner for as long as I can remember.

I started going there as a teenager. After evening study sessions, my friends and I would walk there with almost no money and share one bowl of noodles between three of us. These days I go whenever I'm back home, usually with my parents. My dad insists on buying the same roasted sweet potatoes every time, and my mum spends ages chatting with a stallholder she's known for twenty years.

I like it so much partly because the food is genuinely good and cheap, which is rare nowadays. But more than that, it's full of memories. Walking through it, I feel like a teenager again, worrying about exams and dreaming about the future. I also love the fact that it hasn't become a polished tourist attraction. It's still a place where local people go to eat, gossip and unwind at the end of the day, and I really hope it stays that way.

part3.q: Why are markets still popular when there are so many supermarkets?
part3.sample: Markets offer things supermarkets can't, especially freshness and personal contact. At a wet market, the vegetables were often picked that morning, and you can bargain or ask the seller how to cook something. Older people in particular enjoy the social side, since they see the same stallholders every day. Markets also feel lively and unpredictable. For tourists, they're a window into local life that a supermarket chain, which looks the same in every city, simply can't provide.

part3.q: Should street food stalls be regulated by the government?
part3.sample: To some degree, yes. Food safety is the main concern, because a stall with poor hygiene can make a lot of people ill very quickly. Stalls can also block pavements and leave rubbish behind. However, regulation should be practical. If the rules are too strict or licences too expensive, stall owners, many of whom are on low incomes, will be forced out. A sensible approach is to set aside certain streets and times for markets and give owners basic hygiene training.

part3.q: How do markets reflect the culture of a place?
part3.sample: Quite strongly, I think. The food on sale tells you about local farming, climate and history. A market near the coast is full of seafood, while one in the mountains might sell wild mushrooms and cured meat. The way people behave also says something about the culture, like whether bargaining is expected or how much chatting goes on. That's why wandering around a local market is one of the quickest ways to understand a new place, and it's often more revealing than a museum.

part3.q: Will traditional markets disappear in the future?
part3.sample: Some will, especially in cities where land is valuable and young people buy their groceries on apps. Many old wet markets have already been demolished or moved indoors. But I don't think markets will disappear entirely. Night markets and weekend craft markets are actually becoming more popular, because people want experiences rather than just products. The markets that survive are likely to be those offering atmosphere, local culture and things you can't easily order online.

cueCard.title: Describe a place where you often do exercise.
cueCard.final: and explain why you like exercising there.

sample:
The place I'd like to talk about is a public sports centre about ten minutes' walk from my office. It was built a few years ago by the district government, and it's housed in a large, rather plain grey building next to a secondary school.

It has much better facilities than you'd expect from the outside. On the ground floor there are eight badminton courts and a basketball court, and upstairs there's a small gym, a table tennis hall and a studio for yoga and dance classes. There's also an outdoor running track, which the school uses during the day. Prices are reasonable because it's partly subsidised, though you have to book courts through an app a few days in advance, especially for evenings.

I go there every Wednesday evening to play badminton with a group of colleagues. We book two courts from seven to nine and usually play doubles, swapping partners after every game so it doesn't get too competitive. Occasionally I also use the running track at lunchtime when I'm training for a race, although in summer it's far too hot for that.

The main appeal is convenience. Because it's so close to work, there's no excuse to skip a session. I also like the relaxed atmosphere. Unlike some expensive private gyms, nobody is showing off, and you see everyone from schoolchildren to retired couples playing side by side. Most importantly, though, it's where I switch off. After a stressful day of meetings, chasing a shuttlecock for two hours is the best way I know to clear my head.

part3.q: Why don't some people do enough exercise?
part3.sample: Time is the excuse people give most often, and for workers with long hours and commutes, it's a genuine problem. But I think motivation is the deeper issue. Exercise often feels like hard work with rewards that only appear much later, whereas scrolling on a phone gives instant pleasure. Cost and access matter too. Gym memberships can be expensive, and not every neighbourhood has safe places to walk or run. People who never enjoyed sport at school may also feel awkward starting as adults.

part3.q: Should the government provide free sports facilities?
part3.sample: Basic facilities, yes, like outdoor courts, running paths and exercise equipment in parks. A healthier population puts less pressure on hospitals, so it's a sensible investment. However, it would be difficult to make everything free, because indoor centres are expensive to run and maintain. A mixed system seems fairer, where simple facilities are free for everyone and specialised ones charge a modest fee, with discounts for students and pensioners.

part3.q: Is it better to exercise alone or with other people?
part3.sample: Both have their advantages. Exercising alone is flexible, since you can go whenever you like and focus entirely on your own goals, and it can be a good time to think things through. Exercising with others, on the other hand, keeps you accountable, because it's much harder to skip a session when friends are expecting you. Group activities also add a social element, which makes exercise feel less like a duty. Personally, I find a combination works best.

part3.q: How will people's exercise habits change in the future?
part3.sample: I think technology will play a bigger role. Wearable devices already track steps and heart rate, and future versions might give personalised training advice in real time. Home workouts using screens or virtual reality could become more popular, particularly for busy people. At the same time, as societies age, gentler forms of exercise like walking groups and tai chi may grow. Ideally, employers will also encourage more movement at work, because sitting at a desk all day is a serious health problem.

cueCard.title: Describe a piece of clothing you often wear.
points: when and where you got it
cueCard.final: and explain why you like wearing it.

sample:
The piece of clothing I'd like to describe is a dark green waterproof jacket. It's quite lightweight, with a hood that folds into the collar and plenty of pockets. It's not particularly fashionable, but I probably wear it more than anything else I own.

I bought it about four years ago, during my final year at university, before a trip with the university hiking club. We were heading to a mountain area where the weather can change very quickly, and the club leader warned us that a cheap raincoat wouldn't be enough. I went to an outdoor equipment shop and spent far more than I'd planned, which felt painful on a student budget. On that first trip, it rained almost non-stop for two days, and I stayed completely dry while some of my friends were soaked, so I knew straight away it had been worth it.

Since then, it's become my go-to jacket for almost everything. I wear it for hiking, of course, but also on rainy days in the city, which are pretty frequent where I live. It's ideal for photography walks too, because I can keep spare batteries and a lens cloth in the pockets.

I like wearing it mainly because it's so practical. It's light enough to stuff into a backpack, yet it keeps out wind and heavy rain. The colour suits me as well, since dark green is my favourite and it hides mud nicely. Above all, though, it's full of memories. There's a tiny burn mark on one sleeve from a campfire, and every time I notice it, I'm taken back to that first trip.

part3.q: Why do some people spend a lot of money on clothes?
part3.sample: For some people, clothes are a way of expressing who they are, so they're willing to pay for quality or a particular style. Others buy expensive brands to show status, because a famous logo signals success. Social media has intensified this, since people want to look good in photos and don't like being seen in the same outfit twice. And in certain jobs, like sales or law, looking smart can genuinely affect how clients and colleagues treat you.

part3.q: What problems does fast fashion cause?
part3.sample: The biggest problem is waste. Clothes are now so cheap that many people wear something a few times and then throw it away, and huge amounts end up in landfill. Producing them also uses enormous amounts of water and chemicals, which pollute rivers in the countries where they're made. There are human costs too. Factory workers are often paid very little and work in unsafe conditions so that brands can keep prices low. Shoppers rarely see any of this.

part3.q: Do the clothes people wear affect how others judge them?
part3.sample: Yes, whether we like it or not. First impressions are formed in seconds, and clothing is one of the first things people notice. Someone in a suit might be assumed to be more competent, while someone in scruffy clothes could be treated with less respect in a shop or at a job interview. Of course, these judgements are often unfair and inaccurate. But because they're so common, it's sensible to dress appropriately for important situations.

part3.q: How might clothing change in the future?
part3.sample: I think clothes will become smarter and more sustainable. There are already jackets that can heat up and fabrics that monitor your heart rate, and these will probably become cheaper and more common. Environmental pressure is likely to push brands towards recycled materials and repair services. We might also see more clothing rental, where people pay a monthly fee to borrow outfits rather than buying them. If that happens, owning a huge wardrobe may start to seem old-fashioned.

cueCard.title: Describe something you bought but did not use as much as you expected.
points: when and where you bought it
cueCard.final: and explain why you did not use it very much.

sample:
I'd like to talk about a folding exercise bike that I bought about a year and a half ago. It's a compact black machine with a small screen showing your speed and distance, and it folds up so you can store it in a corner. In theory, it was perfect for a small flat.

I bought it online during one of the big shopping festivals in November, when almost everything is heavily discounted. That year had been particularly rainy, and I'd missed a lot of my evening jogs, so I'd been thinking about getting some indoor equipment. Then an advert for this bike kept appearing in my social media feed, showing a smiling woman pedalling away in a tiny, beautifully decorated flat while watching a film. It was thirty per cent off, and I persuaded myself it would pay for itself compared with a gym membership.

For the first couple of weeks, I used it almost every evening. But then the problems started. It was much noisier than I'd expected, and since my flatmate's bedroom is right next to the living room, I couldn't use it late at night. It was also surprisingly boring. Cycling for half an hour while staring at a wall is nothing like riding outdoors. Gradually, I went from using it daily to weekly, and then hardly at all.

Now, I'm embarrassed to say, it's mainly used for drying clothes. Looking back, I bought it for the person I wanted to be rather than the person I actually am. I prefer exercising outdoors and with other people, and no discount could change that. It's a lesson I try to remember whenever a sale starts.

part3.q: Why do people often buy things they don't need?
part3.sample: Retailers are very good at creating a sense of urgency. Limited-time discounts and countdown clocks make people feel they'll lose out if they don't buy immediately. Shopping can also be emotional. After a stressful day, buying something gives a small burst of pleasure, even if the feeling fades quickly. And as I found out myself, people often buy things for an imagined future self, someone fitter or more organised, rather than for the life they actually lead.

part3.q: Are big online shopping festivals good for consumers?
part3.sample: They're good in a narrow sense, because people can save money on things they were going to buy anyway. Some families wait for these sales to buy expensive items like fridges or laptops. But the overall effect is probably negative. The discounts are often confusing, with complicated rules about coupons, and some sellers even raise prices beforehand. More importantly, these events encourage impulse buying on a huge scale, which leads to waste and, for some young people, credit card debt.

part3.q: Why has buying second-hand become more popular among young people?
part3.sample: Partly it's about money. Living costs in big cities are high, and buying second-hand lets young people get decent furniture, electronics or clothes for a fraction of the price. Apps have also removed the old embarrassment, since browsing used items on a phone feels just like ordinary online shopping. Environmental awareness plays a role too, as many young people dislike the idea of perfectly good things being thrown away. And some simply enjoy hunting for something unique that nobody else has.

part3.q: Will people buy fewer things in the future?
part3.sample: It's hard to say. On the one hand, there's growing awareness of environmental problems, and some young people are choosing a minimalist lifestyle, owning fewer but better things. Rising housing costs also mean smaller homes with less space for possessions. On the other hand, online shopping keeps getting faster and more persuasive, and economies depend on people spending. My guess is that people will spend more on experiences and services, like travel and courses, rather than physical goods.

cueCard.title: Describe a picture or painting that you have in your home.
cueCard.final: and explain why it is important to you.

sample:
I'd like to talk about a drawing that hangs on my bedroom wall. It's an ink drawing of the old building where I lived as a child, and it was drawn by my younger cousin Xiaoyu, who's an extremely talented artist for a teenager.

The picture shows our old six-storey block from across the street on a summer evening. It's full of tiny details that only someone who knew the place would include, like washing hanging from the balconies, a row of bicycles by the entrance and the old camphor tree that shaded the yard. In one of the third-floor windows, he even drew a small figure doing homework at a desk, which he says is me.

He gave it to me for my birthday last year. Months earlier, I'd shown him some old photos of the building and mentioned how much I missed it, since it was knocked down about ten years ago. I had no idea he'd been secretly working on it for weeks, using the photos and my parents' memories. When I unwrapped it, I was completely lost for words.

It's important to me for two reasons. To begin with, it's the only picture that really captures how it felt to live there, the noise, the neighbours and the closeness. Photos show what the building looked like, but his drawing shows what it meant. It also represents a bond between me and my cousin. He's usually very quiet, so I see it as his way of saying something he'd never say out loud. I had it properly framed, and it's the first thing I see every morning.

part3.q: Why do people like to decorate their homes with pictures?
part3.sample: Pictures make a house feel like a home. Bare walls can look cold and temporary, whereas a painting or a few photos give a space personality. People also choose pictures that remind them of people, places or moments that matter to them, so the walls become a kind of personal history. For others, it's about mood. A calm landscape in a bedroom or a colourful print in a kitchen can noticeably change how a room feels.

part3.q: Why are some famous paintings so expensive?
part3.sample: Partly because they're unique. There's only one original, and when lots of wealthy collectors want the same thing, prices rise dramatically. The artist's reputation and the painting's history also add value, especially if it's linked to an important period. But I suspect a lot of it has little to do with art itself. For very rich people, famous paintings are investments and status symbols, a bit like gold, and they often end up locked away in storage rather than on display.

part3.q: Should art be displayed in public places, such as streets and stations?
part3.sample: I think so. Most people rarely visit galleries, so public art is one of the few ways art reaches everyone, regardless of income or education. A mural or sculpture can brighten up a dull area and give a neighbourhood its own identity. Some metro stations in Chinese cities now have artworks reflecting local history, which I find quite charming. Of course, the art should be chosen carefully, ideally with input from residents, because anything paid for with public money should mean something to the public.

part3.q: Will artificial intelligence change the way people create art?
part3.sample: It's already changing it. AI tools can produce impressive images in seconds, which is worrying for illustrators whose work has been used to train these systems, often without permission. On the other hand, some artists use AI as a starting point, a bit like a sketchbook, and then develop the ideas themselves. I suspect human-made art might become more valued, not less, precisely because it takes time and reflects a real person's experience. People may well pay more to know something was made by hand.

cueCard.title: Describe a ceremony that was important to you.
points: when and where it took place
cueCard.final: and explain why it was important to you.

sample:
I'd like to talk about my university graduation ceremony, which took place about three years ago on a very hot morning in June. My university is more than a thousand kilometres from my hometown, so it meant a lot that my parents managed to come at all.

The ceremony was held in the university's main sports hall. There were around two thousand graduates in black gowns and square caps, all sweating heavily because the air conditioning could barely cope. The president gave a long speech, and then each of us walked across the stage to have the tassel on our cap moved from one side to the other, which symbolises becoming a graduate. It took hours, but nobody seemed to mind.

My parents had travelled overnight by train and sat near the back of the hall. My mum had bought a new dress especially for the day, and my dad, who almost never takes photos, had borrowed a camera from a neighbour. Afterwards, we wandered around the campus taking pictures in front of the library, the lake and my old dormitory, before having a big lunch near the south gate.

It mattered to me because it marked the end of four years of hard work and the start of my working life. But it was also the first time my parents had seen my university, the place I'd been describing on the phone for years. Watching my dad photograph everything so carefully, I realised how proud he was, even though he didn't say much. It's one of the few times I've seen him so emotional.

part3.q: Why are ceremonies important in people's lives?
part3.sample: Ceremonies mark transitions. Life changes gradually, and without a clear moment to recognise that something has ended and something new has begun, those changes can pass almost unnoticed. A graduation or a wedding gives everyone, not just the people involved, a chance to stop and reflect. Ceremonies also bring families together and connect us with tradition, since many rituals have been repeated for generations. That sense of continuity can be very comforting at emotional times.

part3.q: Why do some young people prefer simpler ceremonies than their parents' generation did?
part3.sample: Some of it is about money. Elaborate weddings and banquets cost a fortune, and many young couples would rather put that money towards a flat or travel. But there's also a shift in values. Older generations often saw ceremonies as a way to display the family's status to relatives and colleagues, whereas young people tend to want something personal that reflects their own tastes. They also worry less about what distant relatives think, which gives them more freedom to break with tradition.

part3.q: Should schools hold ceremonies to celebrate students' achievements?
part3.sample: Generally, yes, as long as they're inclusive. Recognising effort publicly can motivate students and give them memories they'll keep for life. A graduation ceremony, for example, marks something every student has worked towards. The risk comes with award ceremonies that only celebrate the top few, which can make everyone else feel like a failure. Schools should recognise a range of achievements, such as improvement, kindness or creativity, rather than just exam results.

part3.q: Why do people often feel emotional at ceremonies?
part3.sample: Partly because ceremonies make us aware of time passing. At a graduation, parents suddenly see their child as an adult and remember all the years it took to get there. The rituals themselves, like music, speeches and formal clothes, are designed to create a sense of occasion, which heightens emotions. Being surrounded by others who feel the same way also makes it easier to let feelings show. And ceremonies often remind us of people who are no longer there to share the moment.

cueCard.title: Describe an exhibition you visited.
points: when and where you saw it
cueCard.final: and explain what you learned from it.

sample:
I'd like to talk about an exhibition on the history of the river that runs through my city. It was held at the city museum last spring, and I went with my parents, who were visiting me for a long weekend. I'd chosen it partly because I thought it would interest my dad, who loves anything to do with boats and engineering.

The exhibition traced how the river had shaped the city over roughly two thousand years. The first rooms had ancient pottery and coins found in the riverbed, along with a model of a wooden cargo boat from about a thousand years ago. Later sections covered the busy docks of the early twentieth century, with old photographs of workers carrying sacks of rice on bamboo poles. The final part was more interactive. There was a huge digital map on the floor, and as you walked across it, it showed how floods had reshaped the riverbanks over the centuries.

What I remember best, though, was a small corner with recorded interviews with elderly residents. One woman described washing clothes in the river as a girl, and an old dock worker talked about the day the last cargo pier closed. My dad stood listening to them for ages.

I learned a surprising amount. I had no idea that the city had been badly flooded twice in the last century, or that the park near my flat was once one of the busiest docks in the region. More than the facts, though, it changed the way I see the river. Now, when I jog along it, I sometimes think about all the people who worked there long before me.

part3.q: Why do some people prefer interactive exhibitions to traditional ones?
part3.sample: Interactive exhibitions let people learn by doing rather than just reading labels, which tends to make information more memorable. They're especially popular with families, because children can touch, play and explore instead of being told to keep quiet. Adults who aren't confident about history or science also find them less intimidating. However, there's a risk of turning museums into amusement parks, where people press buttons and take selfies without really thinking about what they're seeing.

part3.q: Is it important for people to learn about the history of the place where they live?
part3.sample: Yes, very much so. Knowing the history of your area helps you understand why it looks the way it does, why certain foods are popular or why streets have particular names. It can also give people a stronger sense of belonging, which matters in cities where many residents have moved from elsewhere. And local history often teaches broader lessons, for example about how earlier generations coped with floods, poverty or rapid change.

part3.q: Should museums be designed mainly for tourists or for local people?
part3.sample: Ideally both, but I'd put local people first. Tourists usually visit once, whereas residents can return many times, bring their children and feel that the museum belongs to them. If an exhibition only shows famous highlights for visitors, it can feel shallow. Then again, tourism brings in money that keeps museums running, so it makes sense to offer multilingual guides and good facilities. The best museums manage to tell local stories in a way that outsiders can also appreciate.

part3.q: How will technology change the way people visit exhibitions in the future?
part3.sample: Exhibitions will probably become much more immersive. Virtual and augmented reality could let visitors step into a historical street scene or watch an ancient object being made. Personalised audio guides might adjust the information to each visitor's interests and level of knowledge, and some people will explore exhibitions entirely online from home. Still, I believe the physical experience will remain valuable, because standing in front of a real object that's hundreds of years old creates a feeling no screen can replace.

cueCard.title: Describe a party that you enjoyed.
points: when and where it was held
what people did at the party
cueCard.final: and explain why you enjoyed this party.

sample:
The party I'd like to describe is a housewarming party that my flatmate and I threw when we moved into our current flat, about two years ago. Neither of us had ever hosted anything bigger than a dinner for three or four people, so we were both a bit nervous.

We invited about fifteen people altogether, a mix of colleagues, friends from my badminton group and a few of my flatmate's old classmates. Hao came along with his daughter, Duoduo, who was only three at the time and fell asleep on our sofa halfway through. Since our kitchen is so tiny that two people can't cook in it at the same time, we decided on hot pot, which was the perfect solution. We borrowed two extra pots, and everybody brought something to throw in, from sliced lamb to tofu and mushrooms.

Most of the evening was spent around the table, eating, talking and laughing. After dinner, someone suggested a game where you have to guess what other people are drawing, and it got surprisingly competitive. My colleague Fang, who's a designer, was unbeatable, which everyone agreed was rather unfair. Later on, a few of us went out onto the balcony to look at the lights along the river, and we stayed there chatting until well after midnight.

I enjoyed it because it brought together people from different parts of my life who'd never met before, and they got on remarkably well. It also made the flat feel like a real home rather than just somewhere we rented. And honestly, it was a relief that nothing went wrong. Even the washing-up the next morning didn't seem too bad.

part3.q: Why do people like to have parties?
part3.sample: Parties give people a reason to break their routine and spend relaxed time with others, which busy adults rarely do otherwise. They also mark occasions, so the party becomes a way of saying that a birthday or a new home matters. For hosts, there's the pleasure of bringing their friends together and looking after them. And for people who are new to a city, parties are one of the easiest ways to meet others and build a social circle.

part3.q: Do people in your country prefer to celebrate at home or in restaurants?
part3.sample: Increasingly, in restaurants. Flats in big cities tend to be small, and many people work long hours, so preparing food for a group at home feels like too much effort. Restaurants offer private rooms, so you get space and service without any washing-up. Even so, home gatherings are still common in smaller towns and within families, especially at Spring Festival, when cooking together is part of the tradition. Among young people, hot pot at home has become a popular compromise.

part3.q: Is it important for children to go to parties?
part3.sample: I think it's good for them, within reason. Parties teach children social skills, such as sharing, taking turns and talking to kids they don't know well. They're also simply fun, and childhood should include plenty of that. However, some parents now organise very expensive, elaborate parties that put pressure on other families to compete. A simple gathering with games and cake is probably just as valuable, because the focus stays on playing together rather than impressing anyone.

part3.q: Why do some people dislike going to parties?
part3.sample: For introverts, parties can be exhausting rather than relaxing. Making small talk with strangers for hours drains their energy, even if they enjoy their friends' company in smaller groups. Others feel anxious in noisy, crowded rooms where they don't know anyone. There can be practical reasons too, such as the cost of travel or simply being too tired after a long working week. I don't think that's a problem, though. Not everyone needs to love parties to have a good social life.

cueCard.title: Describe a time when you were late for something important.
cueCard.final: and explain how you felt about being late.

sample:
I'd like to talk about the time I missed my train home for the Spring Festival, about two years ago. For most Chinese people, getting home for the New Year is the year's most important journey, and tickets are so hard to get that I'd set an alarm to book mine the moment sales opened.

My train was due to leave at ten past three in the afternoon. I'd planned to leave work at lunchtime, but just as I was packing up, my manager asked me to fix an urgent problem with a client's campaign. It took longer than I'd hoped, and by the time I got onto the metro, I had less than an hour. Then, two stops from the station, the metro stopped in a tunnel because of a signal failure, and we sat there for nearly twenty minutes. I kept checking the time, but there was nothing I could do. When I finally ran into the station, the gates had closed two minutes earlier.

Luckily, the station staff were very understanding and helped me change my ticket, but the only seat left was on a much slower overnight train, which meant arriving home nine hours later than planned. My parents had prepared a big dinner for my arrival, and they ended up keeping it warm until the early hours.

At the time I felt awful, mainly because I'd let my parents down. Looking back, though, it taught me a valuable lesson about leaving a buffer. These days, I aim to arrive at the station at least an hour early, and I never agree to last-minute work on travel days.

part3.q: Why are some people always late?
part3.sample: Often it's simply poor planning. Some people underestimate how long things take, like getting ready or travelling across town, and they don't allow for delays. For others, it's about personality. They try to squeeze in one more task before leaving, because they hate wasting even a few minutes waiting. In some cases, being late is a sign that someone doesn't value the event or the people involved very much, which is why it can come across as disrespectful.

part3.q: Is punctuality more important in some situations than in others?
part3.sample: Definitely. For a job interview, a flight or a medical appointment, being late can have serious consequences, so punctuality is essential. In business, too, arriving late for a meeting with a client can damage trust. Social situations are usually more flexible. If you're meeting a close friend for coffee, a few minutes either way doesn't matter much. Cultural expectations vary as well. In some countries, arriving exactly on time for a dinner party is actually considered slightly rude.

part3.q: Has technology made people more or less punctual?
part3.sample: In some ways, more punctual. Navigation apps tell us exactly when to leave and warn us about traffic, and digital calendars send reminders before every appointment. However, technology has also made people more relaxed about being late, because it's easy to send a quick message saying you're running ten minutes behind. In the past, if you were late, the other person had no idea whether you were coming at all, so there was more pressure to be on time.

part3.q: How do attitudes to time differ between generations?
part3.sample: Older people in my country tend to be very punctual, often arriving early, partly because they grew up without mobile phones, when plans had to be fixed in advance. Younger people are more flexible and often make or change plans at the last minute. They also see time differently at work. Many young employees care more about flexible hours and results than simply being present at a desk, whereas their parents' generation often equated long hours with hard work.

cueCard.title: Describe a time when you taught someone how to do something.
points: what you taught him or her
cueCard.final: and explain how you felt about the experience.

sample:
I'd like to talk about the summer before I started university, when I taught my grandmother on my mum's side how to use a smartphone. She was in her mid-seventies and lived with my grandfather in a small town, and the whole family was keen for her to be able to video-call us. My grandfather had no interest in phones whatsoever, but she was curious.

My uncle had bought her a phone, but it had been sitting in its box for weeks, because she was convinced she'd break it. Since I had nothing to do that summer after the entrance exam, I went to stay with them for a fortnight, determined to change that.

I quickly realised that the usual way of teaching wouldn't work. When I showed her things quickly, she'd nod politely and forget them immediately. So I slowed right down. First, I removed every app she didn't need and made the text and icons as large as possible. Then I wrote step-by-step instructions in big characters in a little notebook, with drawings of each button. We practised one skill a day, like answering a call or sending a voice message, and I made her do everything herself while I sat on my hands.

By the end of the fortnight, she could video-call my mum and send photos of her vegetable garden. I felt prouder than I had about my exam results. It also taught me a lot about patience, because things that seem obvious to young people aren't obvious at all if you've never used a touchscreen. Now she video-calls me every Sunday, usually to tell me I look tired.

part3.q: Why is it sometimes difficult to teach people you know well?
part3.sample: Because the relationship gets in the way. With family members, there's often a lot of history, so a small correction can be taken as criticism, and people lose patience with each other much faster than they would with a stranger. Parents teaching their teenagers to drive is a classic example. There can also be awkward role reversals, like a grandchild teaching a grandparent. A professional teacher has emotional distance, which makes it easier to stay calm and stick to the lesson.

part3.q: Should young people be responsible for helping older relatives with technology?
part3.sample: To some extent, yes. Young people are usually the most comfortable with technology, and helping elderly relatives is a natural way of giving something back. It can strengthen relationships between generations, too. However, it shouldn't all fall on families. Many older people live far from their children, and some have no family at all. Banks, hospitals and government services should design their apps to be simpler and keep offline options available, so that nobody is left behind.

part3.q: What skills do you think everyone should learn?
part3.sample: Apart from reading and maths, I think everyone needs basic financial skills, like managing a budget and understanding loans, because many adults get into debt simply through a lack of knowledge. First aid is another, since it can genuinely save lives. Cooking a few healthy meals is useful too. And these days, being able to judge whether information online is reliable might be one of the most important skills of all, given how quickly misinformation spreads on social media.

part3.q: Will people learn practical skills differently in the future?
part3.sample: Very likely. Video tutorials have already transformed how people learn things like repairing a bike or cutting hair, and they're free and available at any time. In the future, augmented reality glasses might guide you step by step, showing exactly where to put your hands, and AI tutors could give instant feedback. Nevertheless, I suspect some skills, especially ones involving touch or judgement, like cooking or woodwork, will still be learned best from a real person standing beside you.

cueCard.title: Describe a song that is special to you.
cueCard.final: and explain why this song is special to you.

sample:
The song I'd like to talk about is a Chinese folk song called Jasmine Flower. It's very old, probably a couple of hundred years at least, and it's one of the best-known Chinese songs abroad. Apparently, an Italian composer even borrowed its melody for one of his operas.

I first heard it as a small child, from my grandmother on my dad's side. She used to sing it while she was cooking or hanging out the washing, always very softly, almost under her breath. I didn't understand the words at the time. I just remember the melody, which rises and falls gently, a bit like someone strolling slowly through a garden.

The song itself is fairly simple. The singer admires a beautiful jasmine flower and wants to pick one, but hesitates, partly because the flower is so lovely and partly out of fear that the person who looks after the garden will scold her. Some people interpret it as a love song, where the flower represents someone you admire but are too shy to approach. I like the fact that it's about holding back, which feels quite Chinese in a way.

It became truly special to me last October, at my grandparents' golden wedding anniversary. After the slideshow of family photos, my grandmother stood up, a little shyly at first, and sang Jasmine Flower in front of everyone. It turned out to be the same song she'd sung at their own wedding fifty years earlier. Everyone stopped eating to listen. Now, whenever I hear it, even as background music in a shopping centre, it takes me straight back to that evening and to her quiet voice in the kitchen.

part3.q: Why do certain songs bring back such strong memories?
part3.sample: Music seems to be closely linked to emotion, so when we hear a song connected with an important period or event, we don't just remember the facts, we feel them again. Songs are also repeated many times, so they become attached to particular stages of our lives, like a summer holiday or a first relationship. Many people find that songs from their teenage years have the strongest effect, probably because emotions are most intense at that age.

part3.q: Are traditional folk songs still important in modern society?
part3.sample: I think they are, even though fewer young people actively listen to them. Folk songs preserve local dialects, stories and ways of life that might otherwise be forgotten. They also give people a sense of shared identity, which is why they're often performed at national celebrations. Interestingly, some young musicians are now mixing folk melodies with pop or electronic music, which introduces them to new audiences. So they're changing form, but they still matter.

part3.q: Why is music so often used in advertising and films?
part3.sample: Because music shapes how we feel almost instantly, often without us noticing. In a film, the right soundtrack can make a scene frightening, romantic or heartbreaking, even if the images stay exactly the same. Advertisers use this too. A cheerful tune makes a product seem fun, while a gentle piano piece makes a brand feel trustworthy. In my job, choosing the music for a campaign video can take longer than writing the script, because it matters that much.

part3.q: Has streaming changed the way people listen to music?
part3.sample: Completely. People now have access to almost every song ever recorded for a small monthly fee, which is amazing. But I think it has made listening shallower. When my parents bought a cassette, they'd play the whole album again and again until they knew every word. Now people tend to skip after a few seconds if a song doesn't grab them, and algorithms decide much of what they hear. Some songs are even written with shorter introductions to stop listeners skipping.

cueCard.title: Describe a TV series you enjoyed watching.
points: how you found out about it
cueCard.final: and explain why you enjoyed watching it.

sample:
I'd like to talk about a Japanese TV series called Midnight Diner. It first came out more than fifteen years ago, but I only discovered it last winter, when a colleague recommended it during a chat about comfort food.

It's set in a tiny restaurant in a back street in Tokyo that's only open from midnight until seven in the morning. The owner, known simply as Master, is a quiet man with a scar on his face. The menu is very short, but he'll cook whatever customers ask for, as long as he has the ingredients. Each episode lasts about half an hour and focuses on one customer and one dish, such as a sweet rolled omelette or sausages cut into the shape of little octopuses. The customers are all kinds of people, from taxi drivers and office workers to struggling singers, and through the food we gradually learn about their lives, their regrets and their small victories.

I watched it one episode at a time before bed, which suited such a gentle show. My flatmate got hooked too, and at weekends we'd sometimes try cooking dishes from the show, with mixed results.

What I loved most was how calm it is. Nothing dramatic happens, but the stories are moving in a quiet way. It also shows how food connects to memory, which really hit home for me, because certain dishes instantly remind me of my dad's cooking. And I like how it treats lonely people with respect. In a big city like mine, lots of people eat alone late at night, and the show makes those moments feel a little less sad.

part3.q: Why do people enjoy TV series about ordinary people's lives?
part3.sample: Because they can see themselves in them. Stories about superheroes or spies are exciting, but series about ordinary people deal with problems we all recognise, like difficult bosses, family arguments or loneliness. That can be comforting, since it reminds viewers they're not alone. These series also tend to be slower and more realistic, which suits people who want to relax after a long day. Small everyday details often feel more truthful than big plot twists.

part3.q: Is binge-watching bad for people?
part3.sample: In moderation, it's harmless, and it can be a nice way to relax at the weekend. The problem comes when it replaces sleep, exercise or time with other people. Streaming platforms deliberately make it hard to stop by playing the next episode automatically after a few seconds, so some people end up watching until three in the morning without really deciding to. It's healthier to treat a series like a book, a chapter or two at a time, so you actually have time to think about it.

part3.q: Why do TV companies often remake popular foreign series?
part3.sample: Mainly because it's less risky. If a show has already succeeded elsewhere, producers know the story works, so they're more willing to invest. A remake also lets them adapt the culture, the humour and the setting for local viewers, who might not enjoy subtitles or understand certain references. However, remakes often disappoint fans of the original, because the charm of a series sometimes comes from exactly the cultural details that get changed.

part3.q: Do TV series influence the way young people behave?
part3.sample: To some extent, yes. Young people often copy the fashion, slang and even attitudes they see in popular series, partly because they identify with the characters. That can be positive, since a series that shows friendship, persistence or kindness can encourage those values. But it can also normalise unrealistic lifestyles, like characters who never seem to work yet live in beautiful flats, or make risky behaviour look glamorous. Parents and schools can help by encouraging young viewers to think critically about what they watch.
